posts.02:
You did the work. The design doc went through three rounds of review, the load tests passed. Then launch day comes and the partner API goes down for six hours.

What stays yours is how you show up the morning after.

Nov 2 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.03:
The migration that drags on for a whole quarter. The on-call week where every alert fires. The reorg that drops you onto a team working in a language you’ve never used.

Which one taught you the most?
posts.04:
The team announces it is breaking up the old monolith. Half the room is excited, half is already drafting objections.

Change is no evil. Staying the same is no good. Try not deciding for a while.

Nov 4 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.05:
Some tech leads review every pull request personally and check the dashboards at midnight in case something moved. It looks like responsibility. Mostly it is fear.

Decide where your hands belong: your code, your reviews, how clearly you write and speak. Let the rest run.
posts.06:
In January the startup closes its round and everyone gets a bigger title. By September half the floor is empty.

When things are going badly, don’t write the ending yet. The wheel that turned against you is still turning.

Nov 6 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.07:
The company gets acquired and your team is dissolved. The title you worked toward vanishes in a reorg. You’re in an interview loop for the first time in eight years.

What you still have is how you think.

Nov 7 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.08:
Not every role on a team is one you would have picked. Someone has to own the billing integration nobody understands.

Nobody gives a talk about that work. It says more about you than any project you got to choose.
posts.09:
Run git blame on a five-year-old project and look for a line from the first commit. Often there isn’t one.

“The universe is transformation: life is opinion.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.3

Nov 9 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.10:
Our tools are new. The people aren’t. The engineer who hoards knowledge so he can’t be replaced, the manager who takes the credit, the team that argues for a month over a naming convention: every one of them has an ancestor in Rome.

Which one have you worked with?
posts.11:
In a short one-on-one, your manager tells you the promotion went to someone else this cycle. You walk back to your desk and the story starts writing itself. They never liked you. Your work doesn’t count.

The disappointment is real. The rest of the weight you can put down.
posts.12:
The postmortem starts and you can feel the room looking for somewhere to put the blame. The vendor’s SDK. The product manager who pushed the date.

The question you can actually answer: what did I decide, and what would I decide differently?
posts.13:
Every company has a channel, or a lunch table, where people go to complain. An hour later nothing has changed, except that you’re a little angrier and so is everyone who listened.

Raising a problem is different. It goes to someone who can act on it, with a proposal attached.
posts.14:
The deploy failed and had to be rolled back. What happened? The deploy failed and was rolled back. That’s the whole fact.

Then come the additions. This is a disaster. I’m going to look incompetent. None of that is in the logs. You wrote it yourself.
posts.15:
Open the dependency file of a project you wrote two years ago. Half the libraries are deprecated. The framework is three major versions behind.

Don’t take it personally when the thing you mastered stops mattering. The habit of learning the next one is what you keep.
posts.16:
The week before your performance review. Half the time you’re imagining the raise. The other half, the meeting where they tell you it isn’t happening.

“You will stop fearing if you stop hoping.”
Seneca, quoting Hecato, Moral Letters 5.7
posts.17:
You’ve just finished a great book on clean architecture and suddenly every pull request on the team looks like a crime scene.

If you’re learning, you notice your own sloppy commits first. If you’re showing off, you only notice other people’s.
posts.18:
The incident report blames the database. Check whether that’s known or just the first plausible guess.

A rational mind, Marcus Aurelius wrote, “assents to nothing false or uncertain.” It reads almost like a checklist.

Nov 18 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.19:
You won’t always feel ready. The 2 a.m. page doesn’t wait for you to feel brave. The meeting where you explain a failure arrives on schedule.

You can walk in reluctant. You just have to walk in.

Nov 19 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.20:
Look closely at your current crisis. A deadline that can’t move. A stakeholder who rewrites the requirements every week. Two senior engineers who won’t speak to each other.

If the situation is old, so are the answers.

Nov 20 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.21:
The afternoon a senior colleague sat with you and explained, slowly, why the bug wasn’t where you were looking. The review where someone pointed out, kindly, that you were optimizing the wrong thing.

Each took minutes. You still carry them. Which one is yours?
posts.22:
The teams hit hardest by an outage are rarely the ones with the worst systems. They’re the ones who never expected the system to fail, so they had no plan for when it did.

Seneca on Fortune: “she is only terrible to those whom she catches unawares.”
posts.23:
The framework you know best becomes the answer to every design question, and any proposal to replace it feels like an insult.

A favorite tool isn’t bad to have. The trouble starts when you can’t be all right without it.

Nov 23 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.24:
The teammate you learn the most from will take another job one day. The product you spent four years on will be shut down by someone who never used it.

If you expect that, you spend more time with that teammate now.

Nov 24 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.25:
The team with an enormous budget that stopped asking whether anything was worth building. The engineer whose stock vested and who now waves pull requests through.

A lean quarter teaches you what matters. A generous one can quietly teach you that nothing does.
posts.26:
Someone from your old cohort is now a director. You find out on a Sunday night while scrolling, and the evening is gone.

“Many grains of frankincense on the same altar: one falls before, another falls after; but it makes no difference.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.15
posts.27:
There’s an argument in the team channel about whether the new lint rule is an outrage. Someone has left a passive-aggressive comment on your design doc. None of it needs you, and all of it is pulling at you.

Mute the channel that exists for arguments.
posts.28:
A new developer on your team keeps making the same mistake: migrations that lock a whole table on deploy. It’s the third time this month.

Maybe nobody ever explained why table locks matter, and all they got was a red X in review.

Nov 28 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.29:
The incident channel at 3 a.m. has its own weather. Someone posts that this is the worst outage in company history. Within ten minutes the panic has more people in it than the fix.

Somebody in that channel needs to stay level.

Nov 29 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
posts.30:
We tend to think calm and action pull in opposite directions.

“He who follows reason in all things is both tranquil and active at the same time, and also cheerful and collected.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.12

Nov 30 · A Daily Thought of a StoicDev
